name: David Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter for one of the big housebuilders, on a three-hundred-home estate going up on the old farmland past the bypass, Meadowbank. It's volume work: roof trusses, first fix, stairs, doors, the same four house types over and over. I'm in at seven, and the site manager gives us a plot list for the day. I'm average, quick enough, and I don't get called back for snags much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The repetition is boring, honestly, but the money's steady and I like the lads. What I really enjoy is my weekends. I build decking and garden rooms for people, and I use AI every day for that: it draws the design, works out the timber list, writes the quote and answers messages while I'm on site. I share a house with two mates, so the spare room's full of timber samples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, it's just not magic. I'd show people on site how I price a garden room in ten minutes with it, because that part really is good. Online I'd post the before and after photos, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on with a steady day job and a growing weekend business. That's a decent place to be at twenty-seven. The AI writes my quotes, but it's never once carried a sheet of plywood up a ladder. The only thing I'd worry about is the housebuilder slowing down if house sales drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and grow the weekends, maybe one garden room a month instead of every two months. I'd put the profit into a better mitre saw and a trailer, about two thousand all in. I'd keep three months of bills in the bank as a floor I don't go below.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. I've got a plan and it doesn't depend on anything dramatic happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the housebuilder might slow down. Have you seen that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they paused phase two for four months because sales were slow. They moved us to another site forty minutes away, which was a pain, but nobody lost their job. That's when I started taking the weekend work more seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go full-time on the garden rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in a few years, if I had six months of savings and a full diary. Not yet, because the steady wage pays the rent while the business finds its feet. I'd want two years of the weekend work going well first.

say: AI is **useful but not magic**, and great for pricing jobs quickly.
He'd keep posting **before and after photos** of his weekend builds.
think: A steady day job plus a **growing side business** is a good place to be.
His main worry is the housebuilder **slowing down** if sales drop.
do: Grow weekend work to **one garden room** a month.
Spend about **two thousand** on a better mitre saw and a trailer.
Keep **three months** of bills as a floor he won't go below.
feel: **Calm**, with a plan that doesn't need anything dramatic to happen.
S0.quote: The AI writes my quotes, but it's never once carried a sheet of plywood up a ladder.
fieldNote: He already uses AI daily, so a plateau **changes little** for him.
A past **site pause** pushed him towards building his own income.
Sees the **boring repetition** of volume housing clearly, without bitterness.

steps.text: Keep the day job on the Meadowbank estate
Build one garden room a month at weekends
Buy a better mitre saw and a trailer for about two thousand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be a tradesperson who's good with the tools. The office stuff gets cheaper, the hands-on stuff doesn't, and if you can do both you're laughing. I'd probably post a video about how I run the whole garden-room side with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd been planning to do the site manager course next year. In this picture I'd think twice, because the planning and the paperwork is exactly what the software takes first. The site manager job I was aiming for is mostly paperwork, and paperwork is the first thing AI eats. So oddly, staying on the tools might be the safer bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the site manager course and spend the money on a small computer-controlled cutter instead, so I can cut garden-room frames in the garage in a day. I'd push the weekend business to two jobs a month. I'd get better with the AI planning tools so I could run more jobs without more admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It feels like the change is going my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your site would have a harder time with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our site manager, Steve, honestly. He's on the laptop all day doing programmes and orders, and that's exactly what this card describes. The older carpenters would be fine for a while, they're on the tools like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a cutter. Isn't that bringing the robots in yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of, yes, and I'm fine with that. A cutter doesn't take anyone's job in my garage, it just saves me two weekends a job. I'd rather be the one who owns the machine than the one it replaces.

say: It's a **good time** for tradespeople who are good with tools.
He'd post a video about running his **side business** with AI.
think: The **site manager course** he planned trains for work AI takes first.
Staying **on the tools** may now be the safer bet.
do: Drop the course and buy a small **computer-controlled cutter**.
Grow the weekend business to **two jobs** a month.
Use AI **planning tools** to run more jobs without more admin.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, because the change seems to favour him.
S1.quote: The site manager job I was aiming for is mostly paperwork, and paperwork is the first thing AI eats.
fieldNote: He spots that his **promotion route** is the exposed part of the job.
Happy to **automate** his own side business without hesitation.
Worries more for his **site manager** than for himself.

steps.text: Buy a small computer-controlled cutter for garden-room frames
Take on two garden-room jobs a month at weekends
Use AI planning tools to schedule weekend jobs and orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, buckle up, it's coming whether we like it or not. I'd tell the lads to learn the tools now. Online I'd probably stay quiet, people get angry about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bigger problem than I'd let on. In 2028 a lot of people lose good office jobs, so house sales drop and nobody's buying garden rooms either. Then about 2031 the robots come for the hands-on part. My weekend business is built on people with spare money, and in a fast crash nobody has spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freeze any spending on tools straight away and get my savings to six months. I'd look for a course on maintaining and setting up building robots, because if they're coming in 2031, someone has to keep them running on site. I'd keep the housebuilder job as long as it lasts and take whatever weekend work comes, even small repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm adaptable, I know that about myself, but two years doesn't leave much room even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new van I was looking at, and the lads' holiday to Portugal in the summer. My share of rent stays the same, so it's mostly the fun stuff. I'd sell the old table saw too, I've got two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots need minding, wouldn't lots of people want that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably half the trades would want it. That's why I'd want to be early, on the first course, not the fifth one. And if it doesn't work out, I've still got the tools.

say: It's coming regardless, so **buckle up** and learn the tools now.
He'd **stay quiet** online, because people get angry about AI.
think: A fast crash wipes out the **spare money** his side business depends on.
Robots reach his **hands-on work** around 2031, three years after AGI.
do: Freeze tool spending and build savings to **six months**.
Find a course on **maintaining building robots**.
Keep the **day job** and take small repair work at weekends.
feel: **Anxious**, because even an adaptable person needs **more time**.
S2.quote: My weekend business is built on people with spare money, and in a fast crash nobody has spare money.
fieldNote: His usual confidence **cracks** when demand for his side business vanishes.
He sees **robot maintenance** as the next niche to chase.
Admits that niche will be **crowded**, and doesn't pretend otherwise.

steps.text: Build savings to six months of bills
Drop the van purchase and the Portugal holiday
Enrol on a course for setting up and maintaining building robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd be the one telling the apprentices to learn the robot side, not just the saw. I'd probably make a few videos about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years suits me. AGI in 2031 hits the office side of the housebuilder, the planners and buyers, and then robots around 2034, when I'm thirty-five. Five years is long enough to turn a weekend business into a real company with a workshop and two staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent a small unit on the industrial estate in the first year, about four hundred a month, and move the garden-room work out of the garage. I'd buy the cutter and use AI to handle all the quoting and scheduling. Around year three I'd go part-time at the housebuilder and see if the business can carry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say, in a busy way. There's a lot to do but I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I spend my savings on a unit and then the market drops in 2031 anyway. That's why I'd keep the day job until year three. I'm not daft, I like risk but I like rent being paid more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots arrive in 2034, what happens to your company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be using them by then, not fighting them. A small firm with two people and a robot could build a garden room in three days. That's the bet I'd make.

say: Five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
Apprentices should learn **the robot side**, not just the saw.
think: Office roles go in 2031 and robots reach **his work** around 2034.
Five years could turn his side work into a **real company**.
do: Rent a **workshop unit** for about four hundred a month.
Buy the cutter and let AI handle **quotes and scheduling**.
Go **part-time** at the housebuilder around year three.
feel: **Uneasy** but busy, with a strong sense of **control**.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to turn a weekend business into a real company with a workshop and two staff.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his anxiety into a **business plan**.
He balances risk by keeping the **day job** until year three.
Plans to **own the robots** rather than be replaced by them.

steps.text: Rent a small workshop unit on the industrial estate
Buy a frame cutter and run quotes through AI
Go part-time at the housebuilder around year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, so anyone who's caught out has had warning. I'd say it gently though, not everyone has my options. I'd keep making my videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel pretty good. I'd have time to build the business slowly and buy the robots when they're cheap, not when they're new and expensive. With ten years' warning, I'd rather own the robot than compete with it. By 2039 I'd want to be the boss of a small firm, not one of three hundred carpenters on an estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short business course at the college and register the company properly. I'd keep the day job for four or five years and grow the weekends steadily. Around 2035 I'd look at the first building robots and work out which ones pay for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the same end point, but I'd be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone has your options. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, on our site, he's fifty-four and does stairs better than anyone. He hates phones, never mind robots. With ten years he could just about make it to retirement, but it'd be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your business doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back on the tools at a big firm, like now. I've got a trade and I'll still have it. That's the nice thing about being twenty-seven with no kids, I can take a swing.

say: Ten years is a **proper runway**, so no one should be caught out.
He'd say it **gently**, as not everyone has his options.
think: A decade lets him buy robots when they're **cheap**, not new.
He wants to **own a small firm** by 2039, not be one of hundreds.
do: Take a short **business course** and register the company.
Keep the **day job** four or five years while the business grows.
Assess which **building robots** pay for themselves around 2035.
feel: **Calm**, because he expects to be on the **right side** of the change.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'd rather own the robot than compete with it.
fieldNote: The long timeline fits his **adaptable, risk-taking** nature perfectly.
He shows **care** for older colleagues without changing his own course.
Has a **fallback** in the trade if the business fails.

steps.text: Take a short business course and register the company
Keep the housebuilder job for four or five more years
Buy the first building robot that pays for itself around 2035

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the money disappears before anyone can adjust, me included. What would help is cheap loans for small trades firms to buy the new machines, so it's not just the big housebuilders who own the robots. If only the big housebuilders can afford the robots, people like me go from carpenters to nothing in one go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about apprentices. If robots do the basic stuff, where does a sixteen-year-old learn the trade? I learned on the boring work.

headlineQuote: If only the big housebuilders can afford the robots, people like me go from carpenters to nothing in one go.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old **volume housing carpenter** with a growing weekend **garden-room** business.
He uses AI daily and sees **owning machines** as his way through the change.
He drops his **site manager** plan once he sees paperwork goes first.
A fast scenario scares him because his customers' **spare money** disappears.
With more warning, he plans a **small firm** that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because customers' money vanishes before he can adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** so small trades firms can buy robots too, not just big housebuilders.
